articles.title: With Export Controls, Nvidia, AMD, & Intel Lose Much More Than Sales
articles.description: Lost sales are but splashy, attention-grabbing headlines that miss the much bigger story.
articles.content: News from China continues to reveal the damage of export controls foisted on U.S. chipmakers by the Biden administration. The controls have in varying ways remained in place under the second Trump adm... [3758 symbols]
articles.summary: The recent news from China has highlighted the impact of export controls imposed on U.S. chipmakers like Nvidia, AMD, Intel and others are being blamed for these needless intrusions. The controls, which have remained in place since the second Trump administration, have been given more life by Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Jim Banks (R-IN), Chuck Shumer (D/NY), Tom Cotton (R/AR), and others. The author argues that focusing on sales lost in the near-term is to miss the larger, long-term impact of these controls. The article also notes that Chinese technology corporations, like Nvidia and AMD, were large buyers of U.K.-produced chips before the last two presidential administrations and Congress adopted protectionism and industrial policy as national security strategies. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) views trade as war rather than what it is, the antidote to war born of the prosperous division of labor. However, the author argues, the worst damage of export control can't be measured in sales, not sales, but in relationships built over time spent on customer knowledge.
articles.shortSummary: Exports controls, imposed by the Biden administration, have significantly reduced American chipmakers like Nvidia, AMD, and Intel's long-term sales potential due to political uncertainty.

Singapore, Malaysia, and Japan data centers face in-person
articles.content: More than half of the Asian companies previously authorized to purchase Nvidia's advanced AI processors have been stripped of that access, according to Reuters reporting via Manila Times first publish... [18348 symbols]
articles.summary: Novision has removed over half of Asian companies previously authorized to purchase Nvidia's advanced AI processors from the market. The move follows a U.S. Commerce Department ruling expanding the reach of AI chip export controls across the Asia-Pacific supply chain. The company introduced a new buyer whitelist requiring companies to undergo rigorous in-person compliance reviews and physically conduct data center visits in three markets, Singapore, Malaysia, and Japan, as critical transit points in the global AI hardware supply chain for suspected chip diversion to China. Companies previously approved to purchase AI accelerators were re-evaluated under more demanding standards and more than half of the former Asian customer base no longer qualified for direct chip purchases. The new buyer blacklist applies to Nvidia's most advanced AI processor, the Blackwell and Hopper families. Companies that fail the initial review can reapply by submitting additional compliance documentation, including ownership structure records and evidence of actual data center capacity, but the threshold for reinstatement is high. The decision to remove these companies from the whitelist was not immediately clear. The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued a guidance notice on May 31, 2026, which addressed a specific vulnerability: whether foreign subsidiaries of Chinese-headquartered companies could legally receive controlled advanced computing chips simply by being incorporated or operating outside China.
articles.shortSummary: Nvidia has reduced over half of Asian AI chip buyers to comply with new export control requirements following a U.S Commerce Department ruling.

The company plans to launch the Ascend 960DT in the first quarter of 2027, three quarters ea... [4909 symbols]
articles.summary: Huawei is accelerating its AI chip roadmap as it seeks to build a stronger domestic alternative to Nvidia. The company plans to launch the Ascend 960DT in Q1 2027, three quarters earlier than its previous target, and the Ascend 970PR in Q3 2027. The revised schedule comes as U.S. restrictions increase on advanced chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Huawei's strategy is to make large numbers of less advanced chips behave more like one enormous computer. Its Peerium Computing Architecture uses UnifiedBus to connect processors with memory, storage and networking hardware, and a new Ascend 960 supernode is designed to connect up to 4,096 processors. However, networking efficiency is a key issue, as communication between machines can consume more than 40% of training time in conventional server systems. The firm has shipped over 1,000 AI computing systems to over 370 customers and has over 5,200 developers working on its Ascend software ecosystem.
articles.shortSummary: Huawei is accelerating its AI chip development, focusing on large-scale, interconnected clusters of chips, amid U.S export controls, to compete with Nvidia's offerings and meet Chinese demand.

articles.content: The United States has approved export licenses worth an estimated $10 billion for Nvidia's H200 AI chips bound for China — and nearly none of those chips have actually arrived. Jeffrey Kessler, the Un... [17135 symbols]
articles.summary: The United States has approved export licenses worth an estimated $10 billion for Nvidia's H200 AI chips bound for China, but nearly none of the chips have arrived. Jeffrey Kessler, the Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, testified before the House Foreign Affairs Committee that while H200 deliveries have technically begun, the volumes remain negligible. This admission highlights the growing gap between paper approvals and real-world enforcement. The Commerce Department added new names to its list of approved Chinese buyers, including ZTE Kangxun Telecom, a unit of ZTE Corp, a company designated as a national security threat under the 2018 National Defense Authorization Act. The licenses represent a significant policy reversal but are still largely symbolic. Chinese firms placed orders for more than two million H200 chips in 2026, while Nvidia held only 700,000 units in stock. The Bureau of Industry and Safety has provided Congress with a confidential list of H200 license applications and their current approval status.
articles.shortSummary: The US approved $10 billion for Nvidia's H200 AI chips, but very few have actually shipped, highlighting regulatory inconsistencies and supply constraints in China.

An Nvidia employee has been charged in Taiwan with smuggling advanced AI chips into China in the first known indictment of a worker at the US chipmaker over illegal exports.

articles.summary: An Nvidia employee has been charged in Taiwan with smuggling advanced AI chips into China, marking the first known indictment of a worker at the US chipmaker over illegal exports. Nine people, including employees of server maker Super Micro Computer, have been charged with illegally selling high-end AI servers to Chinese customers. The alleged scheme involved 130 of Nvidia's flagship B300 servers, a popular server used for training AI models and subject to US export controls. Prosecutors allege that defendants falsely claimed the servers would be used in a data centre in Taiwan, despite its electricity supply and network bandwidth being insufficient. They have requested a maximum sentence of five years in prison for Zhang and three others.
articles.shortSummary: Nvidia employee Zhang was charged in Taiwan with smuggling 130 B300 AI servers into China, defying export controls and damaging the nation’s reputation.
